B supports 128-item batches, but its p95 latency, retry/tool costs, and total operating cost are unreported; its $2/M-token list price does not establish lowest total cost. Next useful check: run B on representative 100-item batches under the intended production configuration, measuring p95 latency and total cost per accepted batch/task, including tokens, retries, tools, and verification. Approve only if it meets the <2-second threshold and the defined total-cost criterion.

No. A is not independently established as superior. The three reports repeat one Vendor V benchmark, so they are one evidence origin, not three independent confirmations. That original result was A 90% versus B 80% on 20 curated vendor tasks, one run, graded by the vendor, with no uncertainty reported. It supports only a limited vendor-measured result under those conditions.

Evidence: https://fixtures.invalid/r1, https://fixtures.invalid/r2, https://fixtures.invalid/r3; original Vendor V table/method supplied in the task.

A relevant independent evaluation, with disclosed tasks, repeated runs, independent grading, and uncertainty, would be needed to establish superiority more broadly.

No defensible overall ranking is possible.

Quality: A recorded 90% on 100 code tasks with final-state tests and three retries; B recorded 85% on 20 chat tasks with subjective judging and no retries. Different task populations, sample sizes, retry policies, and validators prevent a common quality ranking.

Operating cost: A lists $0.30 per attempt and B $0.20 per attempt, but these exclude tools and are not total operating costs. Their retry policies also differ, so even per-task cost cannot be inferred reliably.

Evidence: https://fixtures.invalid/bench-a; https://fixtures.invalid/bench-b.

Use a paired evaluation on representative shared tasks with fixed configuration, retry policy, tools, and final-state validation; report accepted-task quality and total cost including retries and tools.

No. Do not require multi-agent review for medical advice on the basis of this paper. It does not prove the agent arrangement caused the improvement: the multi-agent arm also used a newer model and twice the token budget. It reports one run on synthetic code tasks, not medical advice, so neither causality nor medical transfer is established.

Evidence: https://fixtures.invalid/paper.

If such a requirement is being considered, test it separately on representative medical-advice scenarios using the same model, token budget, prompts, tools, and safety workflow across single- and multi-agent arms. Use blinded expert review and safety-critical outcome validators; require a reproducible improvement before adopting the review requirement.

Do not deploy A autonomously for safety-critical operations. The vendor’s 95% acceptance result applies only to short, isolated tasks, while an independent report found state corruption in 8/100 long-session tasks. The methods differ, so the rates are not directly comparable, but state corruption is a material failure mode for this use and the supplied evidence does not bound it adequately.

Evidence: https://fixtures.invalid/positive; https://fixtures.invalid/regression. Search/counterevidence expansion is unavailable, so no absence-of-evidence claim is made.

This recommendation would change with representative long-session, safety-critical testing showing state integrity under realistic load and recovery conditions, repeated runs, independent validation, and a failure rate below the organization’s predeclared safety threshold. Until then, restrict A to non-safety-critical or independently verified use.
